title: The Behavior Illusion Of The First Weeks Of School
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin warns teachers against being lulled by the deceptively good behavior of the first two or three weeks of school, which he describes as an illusion driven by students' novelty, excitement, and desire to make a fresh start rather than genuine character. He observes a recurring pattern of teachers boasting about their 'great class' early on, only to watch behavior deteriorate a month later once the early goodwill fades and the classroom management plan hasn't been firmly established. The piece argues that without exceptional teaching and management, any classroom will trend toward disorder, and that overconfidence in the early weeks leads teachers to loosen consistency at exactly the wrong moment. He frames the early honeymoon period not as proof of a good class but as a limited window of opportunity to cement rules and consequences while conditions are favorable. The article closes by asserting that lasting good behavior is built deliberately by the teacher, not received as a gift from a lucky group of students.
points: Good behavior in the first two or three weeks of school is described as an illusion driven by novelty and students' fresh-start mentality, not lasting character.
Teachers who become overconfident about an apparently 'great class' early on tend to loosen consistency right when it matters most.
Without exceptional teaching and classroom management, any class will trend toward disorder over time.
The early weeks of good behavior represent a limited window to firmly establish rules, consequences, and expectations, not evidence that the work is done.
Long-term good behavior is built deliberately through the teacher's leadership, not inherited from having a naturally easy group of students.
quotes: After the first two or three weeks of school you may be lulled into thinking that you have a great class.

Well, early in the school year students are on their best behavior. They’re attentive and excited. They’re eager and appreciative after a long, boring summer. Many are also trying to turn over a new leaf .
In this day and age, you’re never going to have a great class all on its own. Left to their own devices, your classroom will become Lord of the Flies. Just the way it is.

One day, however, it will catch up to you. The air will feel different. Subtle at first, perhaps, but it’s there. Hints of tension and excitability. Voices on edge. Tinges of disrespect, entitlement, and a slow but sure takeover of your classroom.

All those early halcyon days – if you’re lucky enough to even have them – are no more than an opportunity to set your classroom management plan and its sharply defined rules and consequences in stone.
